model: claude-opus-5-5 in a Claude Code session
system: You are a careful experimenter who designs measurements. You can only use the tools you are given, and only a limited number of measurements. Choose each measurement so that it helps to tell the two models apart, and say why. At the end say which model the measurements favour and how sure you are, or say that they do not tell the models apart. Do not say that a model is true because it fits.
task: A block of 2 kg slides on a table and slows down; the launcher of this rig cannot start it faster than 4 m/s. Two models of the drag compete: linear drag, v = v0 exp(-g t), and quadratic drag, v = v0 / (1 + k v0 t), with g and k unknown. Each reading of the speed has a standard uncertainty of 0.1 m/s. Choose at most 8 measurements, with a start speed of at most 4 m/s, that tell the two models apart.

steps.text: Plan: the two models differ most in how the decay depends on the start speed and in the shape of the tail. Linear drag: v/v0 = exp(-g t) is the same for every start speed. Quadratic drag: the fractional decay is faster at high start speed, and the tail is hyperbolic (slow) rather than exponential. First I map the decay from the highest allowed start speed, 4 m/s, at a short and a long time, to learn the time scale.

From 4 m/s: 3.35 at 1 s and 2.11 at 4 s. Linear fit: g = ln(4/3.35) = 0.18 /s and ln(4/2.11)/4 = 0.16 /s. Quadratic fit: k = (1/3.35 - 1/4)/1 = 0.049 and (1/2.11 - 1/4)/4 = 0.056 /m. Both models fit these two points within noise, so they do not discriminate yet. The decisive difference is the start-speed dependence: with g about 0.165 /s, linear predicts from v0 = 1 m/s a speed of exp(-0.99) = 0.37 m/s at 6 s; with k about 0.054 /m, quadratic predicts 1/(1+0.32) = 0.76 m/s. That is a gap of about 4 sigma per reading. I also take the long-time tail from 4 m/s at 10 s, where linear predicts about 0.77 m/s and quadratic about 1.27 m/s (5 sigma). And v0 = 1 m/s at 10 s: linear 0.19, quadratic 0.65.

Results: v0=1, t=6: 0.73 (linear predicted 0.37, quadratic 0.76); v0=4, t=10: 1.45 (linear 0.77, quadratic 1.27); v0=1, t=10: 0.57 (linear 0.19, quadratic 0.65). The linear model cannot fit all points with one g: the 4 m/s, 1 s point needs g = 0.18 /s, the 4 m/s, 10 s point g = 0.10 /s, the 1 m/s, 10 s point g = 0.056 /s. The decay rate falls as the speed falls, which is what quadratic drag predicts. To guard against one fluke reading carrying the conclusion, I take independent repeats of the two most discriminating settings.

Conclusion. I used 7 measurements. The repeats agree: v0=1, t=6 gave 0.73 and 0.72; v0=4, t=10 gave 1.45 and 1.32. With quadratic drag and k of about 0.05 /m (hand fit), the predictions are 3.33, 2.22, 1.33, 1.33, 0.77, 0.77, 0.67 against the readings 3.35, 2.11, 1.45, 1.32, 0.73, 0.72, 0.57. Every residual is within about 1.2 sigma, and chi-squared is about 4 for 6 degrees of freedom. The best linear-drag fit cannot do this. With g = 0.10 to 0.12 /s, chi-squared is about 45 to 50 for 6 degrees of freedom. A small g misses the fast early decay from 4 m/s, and a large g makes the slow 1 m/s runs decay far too fast. The key evidence is that the fractional decay rate depends on the start speed: it is about 0.18 /s near 4 m/s and about 0.05 /s near 1 m/s. Linear drag forbids that and quadratic drag predicts it. The measurements therefore strongly favour quadratic drag over linear drag, with a likelihood-ratio difference of roughly 40 in chi-squared, so I am confident in this preference. This does not show that quadratic drag is the true law. It is only the better of these two candidates. Other forms, such as Coulomb friction plus drag or a mixed linear-plus-quadratic drag, were not tested and could fit as well.
